content_voiceover: This is the big-picture synthesis slide, everything you've just learned put onto a single seesaw. On the left, coagulation is pushed up by platelets and plasma clotting factors, and pulled back down by natural inhibitors: tissue factor pathway inhibitor, protein C, antithrombin, and heparin cofactor two. On the right, fibrinolysis is pushed up by the activators t-PA and u-PA, and pulled back down by its own inhibitors, PAI and alpha-2-antiplasmin. Health depends on these two beams staying level relative to each other. If coagulation outweighs fibrinolysis, whether from too much procoagulant drive or too little inhibition, you get thrombosis. If fibrinolysis outweighs coagulation, you get a bleeding tendency. Almost every hemorrhagic and thrombotic disorder in this deck can be mapped back onto which side of this seesaw got knocked out of balance, so it's worth committing this diagram to memory before you move on to hemorrhagic disorders and thrombophilia.
keypoints: Coagulation and fibrinolysis form a balanced, opposing system
Coagulation driven by platelets and plasma factors, checked by TFPI, protein C, antithrombin, and heparin cofactor II
Fibrinolysis driven by t-PA and u-PA, checked by PAI and alpha-2-antiplasmin
Disease states reflect a shift toward thrombosis or toward bleeding
keypoint_voiceover: Keep this seesaw in mind as your framework: platelets and clotting factors push coagulation up, TFPI, protein C, antithrombin, and heparin cofactor two hold it down; t-PA and u-PA push fibrinolysis up, PAI and alpha-2-antiplasmin hold that down, and disease is simply this balance tipping too far one way.
